title: Cryogenic Voltage Control of Magnetism in Silicon-Integrated \newline SrTiO$_3$/Fe Heterostructures
authors: Stijn Reniers, Emile Fourneau, Andries Boelen, Xing-Jian Liu, Ekaterina Gorokh, Lukas Nulens, Vivek Kumar, Luca Ceccon, Christian Haffner, Clement Merckling, Jun-Yi Ge, Bertrand Dupé, Alejandro V. Silhanek, Kristiaan Temst, Joris Van de Vondel
abstract: Cryogenic electronics forms a rapidly emerging research domain for high-performance and power-efficient computing applications. Incorporating nanomagnetic components in cryogenic circuitry adds highly valuable functionality, facilitating downscaling, reducing energy consumption and introducing time-reversal symmetry breaking. Furthermore, low-temperature environments enhance magnetic stability and switching efficiency at nanoscale dimensions, reinforcing the potential of cryogenic nanomagnets. To fully leverage these opportunities, magnetic control schemes require alternative options to current-based writing, which is the main bottleneck regarding power consumption and downscaling. In this regard, voltage-based gating of the magnetic state could drastically enhance operational efficiency and integration density. In this work, we investigate cryogenic Voltage Control of Magnetism (VCM) in epitaxial SrTiO$_3$/Fe thin film heterostructures on a CMOS compatible Si substrate. We demonstrate and quantify voltage-controlled modifications of the magnetic domain structure, consistent with electric field-controlled magnetic anisotropy at the Fe/SrTiO$_3$ interface. These findings provide a viable material system for the development of next-generation magnetic domain-based devices for classical and quantum computing.
summary: This work investigates using voltage control to manipulate magnetism in SrTiO3/Fe heterostructures for next-generation cryogenic electronics. By demonstrating that an electric field can modify the magnetic domain structure, the authors propose a highly energy-efficient alternative to conventional magnetic writing methods. This research establishes a viable material platform for integrating magnetic functionality into low-power quantum and classical computing circuits.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop low-power, scalable magnetic memory elements for cryogenic electronics by replacing high-power current-based writing with voltage-controlled magnetization switching.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated and quantified the Voltage Control of Magnetism (VCM) in epitaxial SrTiO3/Fe heterostructures, showing that back-gate voltage can modify the magnetic domain structure.
method: The study combines experimental characterization (MOKE, SQUID-VSM, MFM) with theoretical modeling (DFT, micromagnetic simulations) to analyze the electric field's influence on magnetic anisotropy.
model_or_system: The physical system is an epitaxial SrTiO3/Fe thin film heterostructure grown on a CMOS-compatible Si substrate, leveraging the ferroelectric/dielectric properties of SrTiO3.
key_observables: Magnetization hysteresis loops (MOKE), domain structure visualization (MFM), effective magnetic anisotropy ($K_{	ext{eff}}$), and the VCM coefficient ($\xi$).
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures, ultrathin Fe film thickness (near the Spin Reorientation Transition, e.g., 0.7 nm), and applied back-gate voltage (V).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on linear approximations for the VCM coefficient ($\xi$) and assumes structural continuity and interfacial quality are maintained during growth.
figures_summary: Figures show sample stacks, $M(H)$ loops varying with thickness and voltage, domain structure images (MFM) showing voltage-dependent domain changes, and theoretical plots relating anisotropy to thickness.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for low-power cryogenic spintronics to selecting the SrTiO3/Fe system, characterizing the magnetic anisotropy dependence on thickness, and finally demonstrating the voltage-tunable magnetic state using multiple characterization techniques.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state spintronics, the underlying mechanism—controlling magnetic order via an electric field coupled to a ferroelectric/dielectric interface—is highly relevant to understanding emergent quantum phenomena in engineered materials.
